messages.content: I want to develop an image segmentation model that distinguishes genuine boundary ambiguity from unfamiliar anatomy under acquisition-domain shift. The targets are unfamiliar-anatomy detection AUROC ≥0.85 on held-out acquisition domains, and boundary-uncertainty Spearman correlation ≥0.6 with inter-annotator disagreement while matching a supervised baseline’s Dice.

That sets out two related but distinct abilities. The model should identify unfamiliar anatomy when acquisition conditions differ, without treating every uncertain boundary as unfamiliar anatomy. Its boundary uncertainty should also track where annotators disagree, while its segmentation Dice matches that of a supervised baseline. The AUROC threshold applies to unfamiliar-anatomy detection on held-out acquisition domains; the Spearman threshold applies to the relationship between boundary uncertainty and inter-annotator disagreement.
What is the distinction between genuine boundary ambiguity and unfamiliar anatomy here?

Genuine boundary ambiguity concerns uncertainty about where a boundary belongs: reasonable annotations may differ even when the anatomy itself is not being treated as unfamiliar. Unfamiliar anatomy concerns whether the anatomy is outside what the model recognizes as familiar. Both could produce uncertainty, but the goal is not to collapse them into a single undifferentiated signal.
And acquisition-domain shift is part of the setting, not another name for unfamiliar anatomy?

Right. Acquisition-domain shift refers to a change in the acquisition domain. The goal is to make the distinction between boundary ambiguity and unfamiliar anatomy under that shift. A change in acquisition conditions does not, by itself, establish that the anatomy is unfamiliar.
How should I read the AUROC requirement?

It requires unfamiliar-anatomy detection AUROC of at least 0.85 on held-out acquisition domains. AUROC measures how well a detection score ranks instances across possible decision thresholds. It does not, on its own, specify performance at any one operating threshold.
Does that tell us whether the ≥0.85 must hold separately for every held-out domain?

The stated requirement says AUROC ≥0.85 on held-out acquisition domains, but it does not specify a per-domain reporting rule or an aggregation procedure. Those details cannot be inferred from the threshold alone.
For boundary uncertainty, why compare against inter-annotator disagreement?

Inter-annotator disagreement provides the stated reference for genuine boundary ambiguity. The required Spearman correlation asks whether higher model-assigned boundary uncertainty tends to correspond, in rank, to greater disagreement among annotators. It does not say that disagreement is a complete account of every possible source of uncertainty.
So Spearman ≥0.6 is about ranked association rather than exact numerical agreement?

Yes. A Spearman correlation of at least 0.6 means the boundary-uncertainty values must have the required rank-based association with inter-annotator disagreement. The requirement does not say their numerical scales must match or that a particular uncertainty value must equal a particular disagreement value.
If the model is uncertain at a boundary, should it necessarily call that anatomy unfamiliar?

No. That would erase the distinction the goal asks the model to make. Boundary uncertainty can reflect genuine ambiguity about placement; unfamiliar-anatomy detection addresses a different question. The goal is to distinguish those possibilities under acquisition-domain shift, not to label all boundary uncertainty as unfamiliar anatomy.
Would the two uncertainty-related targets alone be enough if segmentation quality dropped?

No. The boundary-uncertainty correlation requirement is paired with matching a supervised baseline’s Dice. A model meeting the uncertainty or detection targets but not matching the baseline’s Dice would not satisfy all of the stated requirements.
Does matching the baseline’s Dice mean the model has to produce identical segmentations?

Not necessarily. Dice is a measure of segmentation overlap; matching a supervised baseline’s Dice is a performance comparison, not a claim that the two models must make identical predictions. No numerical tolerance or further comparison rule for “matching” is specified here.
Likewise, could strong Dice by itself demonstrate that the model distinguishes the two kinds of uncertainty?

No. Dice addresses segmentation overlap. It does not by itself establish unfamiliar-anatomy detection AUROC ≥0.85 on held-out acquisition domains or boundary-uncertainty Spearman correlation ≥0.6 with inter-annotator disagreement. The distinction in the goal calls for more than segmentation quality alone.
Is a particular model architecture implied by calling for both detection and boundary uncertainty?

No architecture is specified. The goal describes capabilities and performance requirements: distinguish genuine boundary ambiguity from unfamiliar anatomy under acquisition-domain shift, meet the held-out-domain AUROC target, meet the boundary-uncertainty correlation target, and match the supervised baseline’s Dice. It does not prescribe how the model represents or produces those assessments.
Can I treat the AUROC and Spearman numbers as evidence that the goal has already been achieved?

No. They are targets, not reported results. The statement calls for AUROC ≥0.85 and Spearman correlation ≥0.6, along with matching the supervised baseline’s Dice; it does not say those conditions have already been met.
What is the central point I should keep in mind when discussing the goal?

Keep the two interpretations of uncertainty distinct. The model is meant to recognize genuine ambiguity in boundary placement without conflating it with unfamiliar anatomy, even under acquisition-domain shift. Success also has three stated performance conditions: unfamiliar-anatomy detection AUROC ≥0.85 on held-out acquisition domains, boundary-uncertainty Spearman correlation ≥0.6 with inter-annotator disagreement, and Dice matching a supervised baseline.
For that goal, I propose training a Dice-regularized multi-annotator segmenter with style-invariant anatomy prototypes, and scoring boundary disagreement separately from prototype-distance novelty.

That proposal separates two questions that might otherwise be conflated. The multi-annotator part provides a basis for representing disagreement about boundaries; prototype-distance novelty provides a separate way to score whether anatomy appears unfamiliar. Dice regularization keeps segmentation quality in view during training, while the proposed style-invariant anatomy prototypes are intended to make novelty less dependent on acquisition style.
What does “multi-annotator segmenter” contribute to this idea?

It treats the presence of multiple annotations as relevant to the segmentation model, rather than reducing the boundary question to a single unquestioned outline. In this proposal, that matters because boundary disagreement is meant to have its own score. The phrase does not specify a particular architecture or exactly how the annotations would be combined.
Is boundary disagreement the same score as unfamiliar-anatomy novelty?

No. The proposal explicitly scores boundary disagreement separately from prototype-distance novelty. A boundary-disagreement score concerns ambiguity about boundary placement; a prototype-distance novelty score concerns how unfamiliar the anatomy appears relative to the anatomy prototypes. Keeping them separate is the central distinction in this proposal.
Can you clarify what “prototype-distance novelty” means without choosing a particular implementation?

Conceptually, anatomy prototypes serve as references for familiar anatomy, and novelty is assessed by distance from those references. That describes the role of the score, not the distance formula, how prototypes are learned, or a cutoff for calling something unfamiliar. None of those details is fixed by the proposal.
Why specify that the anatomy prototypes are style-invariant?

Because the setting includes acquisition-domain shift. Calling the prototypes style-invariant expresses the intent that differences in acquisition style should not be mistaken for differences in anatomy when assessing novelty. It is a proposed property of the representation, not an established result or a guarantee that acquisition effects will disappear.
So a large prototype distance is meant to point toward unfamiliar anatomy, not automatically toward an uncertain boundary?

Yes. Prototype-distance novelty is the proposed signal for anatomical unfamiliarity. Boundary disagreement is scored separately, so a large novelty score would not, by definition, be the boundary-disagreement score. The proposal does not specify how either score would be thresholded or interpreted in every individual case.
What does Dice regularization add if the proposal is mainly about those two scores?

It makes segmentation performance part of the training objective rather than focusing only on the distinction between disagreement and novelty. That is important to the stated goal, which also calls for matching a supervised baseline’s Dice. “Dice-regularized” does not specify the regularization weight, the exact objective, or whether the desired Dice performance has been attained.
Could I describe this as a model with one overall uncertainty score that happens to have two explanations?

That would blur the wording of the proposal. It calls for scoring boundary disagreement separately from prototype-distance novelty. You could discuss both as signals relevant to uncertainty, but the proposed distinction is clearer if they remain separate scores rather than being described only as explanations for one undifferentiated score.
Does using multiple annotators establish that every disagreement is genuine boundary ambiguity?

Not by itself. The proposal uses a multi-annotator segmenter and a boundary-disagreement score to address boundary ambiguity; it does not claim that every disagreement must have the same interpretation. Nor does it say that annotator disagreement alone establishes whether anatomy is familiar or unfamiliar.
And do style-invariant prototypes establish that the model will detect unfamiliar anatomy on held-out acquisition domains?

No. They are part of the proposed way to make prototype-distance novelty about anatomy rather than acquisition style. Whether that produces the required unfamiliar-anatomy detection performance on held-out acquisition domains remains an evaluation question, not a conclusion supplied by this proposal.
How much of the training procedure is already specified?

Only its broad structure: train a Dice-regularized multi-annotator segmenter with style-invariant anatomy prototypes, and score boundary disagreement separately from prototype-distance novelty. The proposal does not state a network architecture, loss formula, prototype construction method, training schedule, or score-calibration rule.
Would it be accurate to say the prototypes represent acquisition domains?

Not as stated. They are described as anatomy prototypes, with style invariance as a desired property. Describing them instead as prototypes of acquisition domains would change their proposed role: the novelty score is framed as prototype distance for unfamiliar anatomy, not as distance from an acquisition style.
What if both separate scores are high for the same image or region? Does the proposal rule that out?

No. Separate scoring does not require the scores to be mutually exclusive. It means boundary disagreement and prototype-distance novelty retain distinct interpretations, even if both happen to be high in a case. The proposal supplies no rule for resolving such a case into a single label.
Can I say this approach has already matched the supervised baseline’s Dice?

No. Dice regularization is a feature of the proposed training approach, not a reported performance result. The proposal does not establish that the model has matched the baseline’s Dice or met either of the other performance targets.
Then what is the proposal, stated as precisely as possible without implying a result?

Train a multi-annotator image segmenter with Dice regularization and style-invariant anatomy prototypes. Use separate scores for boundary disagreement and for novelty measured by distance from the anatomy prototypes. This is a proposed way to distinguish ambiguous boundaries from unfamiliar anatomy under acquisition-domain shift; its performance is not specified as an observed result.
Can style-invariant prototypes distinguish unfamiliar anatomy from familiar structures altered by held-out scanner contrast?

They might, but style invariance alone does not guarantee it. The intended distinction is that a change in scanner contrast should not make familiar anatomy appear distant from its anatomy prototype, while genuinely unfamiliar anatomy should remain distinguishable. Whether the prototypes achieve both under held-out contrast is an open question.
Why might a familiar structure look unfamiliar to a prototype-based score?

If scanner contrast changes the appearance features that the score relies on, a familiar structure could end up far from its prototype. The score would then reflect an acquisition-related difference, even though the anatomy is familiar. Calling the prototypes style-invariant expresses the desired resistance to that problem; it does not establish that the resistance is complete.
Would making the representation more invariant necessarily fix that?

Not necessarily. Invariance needs to suppress differences due to scanner contrast without suppressing differences that matter for recognizing anatomy. If both kinds of difference are removed, unfamiliar anatomy could appear close to a familiar prototype. If too little contrast variation is removed, familiar anatomy could still appear novel.
So prototype distance by itself cannot tell me why something is distant?

Right. Distance indicates a difference from the prototypes in the chosen representation; it does not, on its own, identify the cause of that difference. A large distance could be consistent with unfamiliar anatomy, but it could also reflect a familiar structure whose appearance has changed under held-out scanner contrast. The question is whether the representation separates those possibilities well enough.
Does a small distance conclusively mean the anatomy is familiar?

No. A small distance means the representation places it near a prototype. It does not prove anatomical familiarity: the representation could fail to preserve a distinction that matters. The concern works in both directions—contrast-altered familiar anatomy could appear too distant, and unfamiliar anatomy could appear too close.
What exactly would “style-invariant” need to mean for this question?

For this purpose, it would mean that features used for the anatomy comparison remain sufficiently stable when scanner contrast changes, while still retaining features needed to distinguish unfamiliar anatomy. That is a functional description of the desired behavior, not a claim that the prototypes already have it or a specification of how to obtain it.
Is held-out scanner contrast simply another kind of unfamiliar anatomy?

No. Held-out scanner contrast describes an acquisition-related appearance change. The anatomy could remain familiar despite looking different. The question specifically asks whether the prototypes can avoid interpreting that change as anatomical novelty while still detecting anatomy that really is unfamiliar.
Could a prototype be style-invariant for some contrast changes but not for a held-out one?

Yes, conceptually. Style invariance is not automatically unlimited. Behavior under contrast changes the representation has not encountered cannot be inferred merely from the name of the method. The held-out condition matters because it probes whether the intended separation carries over to an acquisition appearance outside those used to form the representation.
How would I phrase the question without assuming a positive answer?

You could ask: “Do style-invariant anatomy prototypes keep familiar structures close to their prototypes under held-out scanner contrast while assigning greater prototype-distance novelty to unfamiliar anatomy?” That keeps the distinction explicit and presents it as something to determine, not something already demonstrated.
Would it be fair to call this a test of whether the novelty score responds to anatomy rather than scanner appearance?

Yes, as a conceptual description. The crucial issue is what drives prototype-distance novelty when contrast changes: anatomical unfamiliarity or acquisition appearance. A score that responds strongly to contrast-altered familiar structures would not, on that basis alone, distinguish the two causes.
Does the separate boundary-disagreement score settle this prototype question?

No. Boundary disagreement addresses uncertainty about boundary placement. The question here is whether prototype distance can distinguish unfamiliar anatomy from familiar anatomy whose appearance has changed with scanner contrast. Keeping the scores separate preserves that question rather than answering it automatically.
If unfamiliar anatomy also changes appearance under the held-out contrast, does that make the distinction impossible by definition?

Not by definition. The representation could, in principle, retain anatomy-related differences while being less sensitive to contrast-related ones. But the combination makes the question more demanding: a novelty score must not treat contrast alone as novelty, and it must not erase the anatomical differences it is supposed to detect. The question does not provide a result either way.
What is the cautious answer, then?

Style-invariant anatomy prototypes are intended to make that distinction possible, but whether they actually distinguish unfamiliar anatomy from familiar structures altered by held-out scanner contrast remains unresolved here. Prototype distance needs to reflect anatomy rather than contrast for the distinction to hold; the description of the prototypes alone cannot establish that it does.
My hypothesis is that style-invariant prototypes achieve unfamiliar-anatomy AUROC ≥0.85 on held-out scanners, with familiar-anatomy false-positive rate ≤10% at 80% sensitivity.

That is a testable hypothesis, not a reported result. It makes two performance claims about distinguishing unfamiliar anatomy from familiar anatomy on held-out scanners: an unfamiliar-anatomy detection AUROC of at least 0.85, and an operating point with familiar-anatomy false-positive rate no greater than 10% at 80% sensitivity.
How does the second condition bear on familiar structures whose scanner contrast has changed?

Those structures are still familiar anatomy. If the novelty score incorrectly treats them as unfamiliar, they contribute to the familiar-anatomy false-positive rate. The ≤10% condition limits that error at the stated 80% sensitivity, without assuming that the condition has been met.
What does 80% sensitivity refer to in this hypothesis?

It refers to detecting unfamiliar anatomy: at the stated operating point, 80% sensitivity means identifying 80% of the unfamiliar-anatomy cases as unfamiliar. The false-positive rate at that same point concerns familiar anatomy incorrectly identified as unfamiliar.
So the ≤10% figure is not a limit on missed unfamiliar anatomy?
Correct. It limits false positives among familiar anatomy at 80% sensitivity for unfamiliar-anatomy detection. The two percentages describe different groups and different errors.
Does AUROC ≥0.85 guarantee that the familiar-anatomy false-positive rate will be ≤10% at 80% sensitivity?

No. AUROC summarizes ranking performance across operating thresholds. The false-positive-rate condition concerns one particular operating point. An AUROC at or above 0.85 does not, by itself, establish that the false-positive rate at 80% sensitivity is at most 10%; the hypothesis specifies both conditions.
Could the operating-point condition hold even if the AUROC target does not?

Conceptually, yes. Performance at one operating point does not determine the whole detection curve or its AUROC. Meeting the ≤10% familiar-anatomy false-positive rate at 80% sensitivity would not alone establish AUROC ≥0.85.
Is AUROC ≥0.85 the same as saying the model classifies 85% of anatomy correctly?

No. AUROC is a measure of how the detection score separates and ranks unfamiliar and familiar anatomy across thresholds; it is not an 85% classification-accuracy claim. The separate 80% sensitivity and ≤10% false-positive-rate figures describe a particular operating point.
Why say “held-out scanners” explicitly?

Because the hypothesis concerns whether the distinction carries over to scanners outside the acquisition conditions used to establish the prototypes. The held-out condition matters to the question of whether scanner-related appearance changes will cause familiar anatomy to appear novel. It does not itself show that the prototypes will generalize.
Does the wording require each held-out scanner individually to reach AUROC ≥0.85?

The hypothesis names held-out scanners but does not specify whether the AUROC and operating-point figures are to be assessed separately for each scanner or through some combined assessment. It would be inaccurate to claim a per-scanner guarantee from the wording alone.
Should I interpret style invariance as the result that makes the numerical targets certain?

No. Style invariance is the intended property of the anatomy prototypes, and the numerical claims are the hypothesis being put forward. Describing the prototypes as style-invariant does not establish AUROC ≥0.85 or familiar-anatomy false-positive rate ≤10% at 80% sensitivity on held-out scanners.
What would a high false-positive rate mean for the distinction we were discussing?

At the stated operating point, it would mean too much familiar anatomy is being flagged as unfamiliar. That would bear directly on the concern that scanner-related changes in familiar structures could be mistaken for anatomical novelty. The hypothesis specifically proposes a familiar-anatomy false-positive rate of no more than 10% at 80% sensitivity.
What if the AUROC target is met but the false-positive rate at 80% sensitivity exceeds 10%?

Then the AUROC part of this hypothesis would be met, but the operating-point part would not. The hypothesis requires both; strong overall ranking would not make the stated false-positive-rate limit unnecessary.
And if the false-positive-rate limit is met but sensitivity is below 80%?

That would not establish the stated operating-point condition. The limit is specified at 80% sensitivity, so a low false-positive rate obtained while detecting fewer unfamiliar-anatomy cases is not the same claim.
Does the hypothesis say the prototypes never confuse unfamiliar anatomy and familiar anatomy?

No. Neither threshold is a claim of perfect separation. The hypothesis allows for detection errors while stating specific proposed performance levels: AUROC ≥0.85 on held-out scanners and familiar-anatomy false-positive rate ≤10% at 80% sensitivity.
How would you state the hypothesis without making it sound like an observed outcome?

The hypothesis is that style-invariant anatomy prototypes will distinguish unfamiliar anatomy on held-out scanners with AUROC ≥0.85 while keeping the familiar-anatomy false-positive rate ≤10% at 80% sensitivity. Whether they do so remains to be determined.

The evaluation activity is to assess prototype-distance novelty on leave-one-scanner-out brain MRI with resection cavities, and report AUROC and familiar-anatomy false-positive rate at 80% sensitivity.

That focuses the evaluation on whether prototype distance separates unfamiliar from familiar anatomy when the scanner is held out. AUROC describes detection performance across thresholds. Familiar-anatomy false-positive rate at 80% sensitivity describes errors on familiar anatomy at a specified sensitivity for detecting unfamiliar anatomy. This is an evaluation activity, not a report of results.
What does leave-one-scanner-out mean in this setting?

Conceptually, a scanner is held out while the novelty score is evaluated on brain MRI from that scanner. The point is to assess performance under a scanner change rather than only under acquisition conditions represented in the non-held-out data. The activity does not specify the number of scanners or how results across held-out scanners would be combined.
Why is the scanner the thing being held out?

Holding out a scanner makes scanner-related acquisition differences part of the evaluation setting. That is relevant to the question of whether prototype distance responds to unfamiliar anatomy rather than simply to changed image appearance. The activity does not presume that the score succeeds in making that distinction.
What role do the resection cavities play?

They specify the brain MRI setting in which prototype-distance novelty is to be evaluated. The activity does not, by itself, define which observations receive the unfamiliar-anatomy label or say that every resection cavity is scored in a particular way. Those details should not be inferred from the mention of resection cavities alone.
Could I describe the task as detecting resection cavities specifically?

That would be narrower than the activity states. It says to evaluate prototype-distance novelty on leave-one-scanner-out brain MRI with resection cavities. It does not explicitly define a cavity-detection task or equate the novelty label with resection cavities in every case.
What exactly is being evaluated: the segmentation or the prototype-distance score?

This activity specifically calls for evaluating prototype-distance novelty. Its named outputs are AUROC and familiar-anatomy false-positive rate at 80% sensitivity, both concerning novelty detection. It does not specify a segmentation-quality result for this activity.
Why report both AUROC and the false-positive rate at 80% sensitivity?

They answer different questions. AUROC summarizes how the novelty score separates categories over a range of possible thresholds. The familiar-anatomy false-positive rate at 80% sensitivity describes how often familiar anatomy is incorrectly flagged as unfamiliar at that particular sensitivity. One figure does not determine the other.
Does 80% sensitivity mean 80% of familiar anatomy is recognized correctly?

No. Here sensitivity refers to detecting unfamiliar anatomy. Familiar anatomy enters the other reported quantity: the false-positive rate, or the proportion incorrectly flagged as unfamiliar at the operating point with 80% sensitivity.
If a familiar structure looks different on the held-out scanner, where would a mistaken novelty call show up?

If that structure is familiar anatomy but the novelty score flags it as unfamiliar, it contributes to the familiar-anatomy false-positive rate. That is why the reported rate is informative in a held-out-scanner setting. The activity does not say how often such mistakes occur.
Does evaluating on a held-out scanner mean the anatomy there must be unfamiliar?

No. Scanner novelty and anatomical novelty are different. A held-out scanner can change image appearance without making a familiar structure anatomically unfamiliar. The evaluation needs that distinction for the familiar-anatomy false-positive rate to be meaningful.
Does leave-one-scanner-out tell us whether the reported AUROC is per scanner or pooled?

Not from this wording alone. It establishes the leave-one-scanner-out evaluation setting, but it does not prescribe whether AUROC is reported separately for each held-out scanner, combined across them, or both. The same reporting detail is unspecified for the false-positive rate.
Is a decision threshold for the novelty score specified?

No numerical score threshold is given. The requested false-positive rate is tied to the operating point at 80% sensitivity, while AUROC considers performance across thresholds. The activity does not specify a threshold-selection procedure.
Would AUROC alone tell us whether familiar anatomy is rarely flagged at 80% sensitivity?

No. AUROC does not fix the false-positive rate at that specific operating point. Reporting the familiar-anatomy false-positive rate at 80% sensitivity makes that particular trade-off visible rather than relying on an overall ranking summary.
Do these instructions say how prototype distance is calculated?

No. They identify prototype-distance novelty as the score to evaluate, but do not give a distance formula, representation, prototype construction method, or scoring granularity. The requested evaluation measures can be described without assuming any of those implementation details.
Could I say that this activity proves the prototypes are style-invariant?

No. The activity is to evaluate the novelty score in a held-out-scanner setting. Such an evaluation bears on how the score behaves under scanner change, but the activity statement contains no findings and does not establish style invariance or detection performance.
What would be an accurate one-sentence description of the activity?

Evaluate prototype-distance novelty on leave-one-scanner-out brain MRI with resection cavities, reporting unfamiliar-anatomy detection AUROC and the familiar-anatomy false-positive rate at 80% sensitivity, without presuming either result.
The leave-one-scanner-out brain MRI evaluation yielded cavity-detection AUROC 0.88 and familiar-anatomy false-positive rate 8% at 80% sensitivity.

Those are two reported results for the held-out-scanner evaluation. The cavity-detection AUROC of 0.88 summarizes how the detection score separates cases across thresholds. The 8% familiar-anatomy false-positive rate describes one operating point: at 80% sensitivity for cavity detection, 8% of familiar anatomy was incorrectly flagged.
Does the AUROC of 0.88 describe performance at that same operating point?

No. AUROC summarizes performance across possible thresholds, whereas the 8% false-positive rate is tied specifically to the operating point at 80% sensitivity. Reporting both gives an overall ranking measure and a measure of errors on familiar anatomy at a specified sensitivity.
When you say 80% sensitivity, what is being detected?

In this reported result, the detection task is cavity detection. The 80% sensitivity refers to detecting cavities at the operating point used to report the familiar-anatomy false-positive rate. It is not a statement that 80% of familiar anatomy was detected.
And what counts as a false positive in the 8% figure?

It is familiar anatomy incorrectly flagged by the detection score at that operating point. The figure is a rate for familiar anatomy, not the percentage of all brain MRI observations that were flagged.
Can I call the 0.88 figure an unfamiliar-anatomy AUROC without qualification?

The precise reported measure is cavity-detection AUROC 0.88. The evaluation concerns prototype-distance novelty in brain MRI with resection cavities, but the result as stated does not establish the same AUROC for every possible form of unfamiliar anatomy. Retaining “cavity-detection” preserves its stated scope.
Does leave-one-scanner-out mean the result was obtained without a scanner being held out?

No. Leave-one-scanner-out means the evaluation involved holding out a scanner. The result is reported for that evaluation setting; the statement does not give the number of scanners, scanner-specific results, or how results across held-out scanners were summarized.
Could the 8% false-positive rate tell us which familiar structures were mistaken for cavities?

Not from the reported figure alone. It quantifies how often familiar anatomy was incorrectly flagged at 80% sensitivity, but it does not identify the structures involved or explain why those errors occurred.
Does this show that scanner contrast had no effect on the novelty score?

No. The results describe detection performance in a leave-one-scanner-out brain MRI evaluation. They do not isolate the effect of scanner contrast or show that the score is wholly insensitive to it. The 8% false-positive rate also indicates that some familiar anatomy was incorrectly flagged at the stated operating point.
Is it possible to derive the false-positive rate at a different sensitivity from these numbers?
No. AUROC 0.88 and one reported operating point do not specify the full detection curve. The false-positive rate at another sensitivity would require information not included in this result.
Do the numbers say how precisely either measure was estimated?
No. The report gives AUROC 0.88 and familiar-anatomy false-positive rate 8% at 80% sensitivity, but no sample counts, uncertainty intervals, or other information about estimate precision.
What can I conclude without extending the result beyond what was measured?

You can report that leave-one-scanner-out brain MRI yielded cavity-detection AUROC 0.88 and familiar-anatomy false-positive rate 8% at 80% sensitivity. Those figures describe this cavity-detection evaluation and its specified operating point; they do not, on their own, quantify performance for other unfamiliar anatomy or explain the causes of individual false positives.
On that basis, I’m deciding to retain prototype-distance novelty scoring for held-out scanners: cavity-detection AUROC 0.88 and familiar-anatomy false-positive rate 8% meet the detection criteria.

That states the decision and its basis precisely. The retained component is prototype-distance novelty scoring for held-out scanners. The supporting detection results are cavity AUROC 0.88 and familiar-anatomy false-positive rate 8% at 80% sensitivity; those figures meet the specified detection criteria in this evaluation.
Why keep both numbers in the rationale rather than just citing the AUROC?

They cover different aspects of detection. Cavity AUROC 0.88 describes separation across thresholds. The 8% familiar-anatomy false-positive rate describes how often familiar anatomy is flagged at the operating point with 80% sensitivity. The decision cites both because the detection criteria concern both overall separation and that operating-point error rate.
What exactly am I retaining?

Prototype-distance novelty scoring for held-out scanners. The decision does not, by itself, select a particular distance formula, change the segmentation component, or specify any additional scoring rule.
Does “meet detection criteria” mean that every objective for the segmentation model is met?

No. It is a conclusion about the stated detection criteria, supported here by cavity AUROC 0.88 and familiar-anatomy false-positive rate 8%. It does not assert a result for boundary uncertainty, inter-annotator disagreement, or Dice relative to a supervised baseline.
Should I call this an AUROC of 0.88 for all unfamiliar anatomy on held-out scanners?

Keep the narrower wording: cavity-detection AUROC 0.88 in the held-out-scanner evaluation. The decision retains prototype-distance novelty scoring for held-out scanners on the basis of that result, but it does not report an AUROC of 0.88 for every kind of unfamiliar anatomy.
How does the 8% familiar-anatomy false-positive rate affect the decision?

It addresses the risk of treating familiar anatomy as novel. At 80% sensitivity in this detection evaluation, the reported false-positive rate for familiar anatomy is 8%, which meets the stated operating-point detection criterion. It is part of the reason given for retaining the novelty score, rather than a claim that false positives never occur.
Does retaining the score mean scanner-related appearance changes have been completely removed?

No. Retaining prototype-distance novelty scoring is a decision based on the stated detection results. Neither cavity AUROC 0.88 nor familiar-anatomy false-positive rate 8% establishes complete invariance to scanner appearance changes or explains every individual score.
Can I say the 8% applies at any sensitivity I choose?
No. The reported 8% familiar-anatomy false-positive rate is at 80% sensitivity. The decision does not provide a false-positive rate at another operating point.
Is the rationale that the cavity AUROC exceeds the AUROC criterion and the familiar-anatomy false-positive rate stays within its limit?

Yes. The cavity AUROC is 0.88 against the detection criterion of at least 0.85, and the familiar-anatomy false-positive rate is 8% against the limit of 10% at 80% sensitivity. Those comparisons explain the statement that the detection criteria are met, while keeping the conclusion tied to the reported cavity evaluation.
Would “retain prototype-distance novelty scoring” imply that boundary disagreement should be scored using prototype distance too?

No. The decision concerns prototype-distance *novelty* scoring for held-out scanners. It does not turn prototype distance into a boundary-disagreement score or merge the two interpretations. Nothing in this decision changes the distinction between anatomical novelty and uncertainty about boundary placement.
Is this a decision to stop evaluating the score?

That is not stated. “Retain” says to keep prototype-distance novelty scoring for held-out scanners on the basis of the detection criteria being met. It does not specify whether any further evaluation will or will not occur.
What is the most careful short formulation of the decision?

Retain prototype-distance novelty scoring for held-out scanners because the reported cavity-detection AUROC of 0.88 and familiar-anatomy false-positive rate of 8% at 80% sensitivity meet the detection criteria. That conclusion is about this novelty-detection decision, not the model’s other performance requirements.
Retaining prototype novelty scoring, I plan to calibrate boundary uncertainty against annotator disagreement on held-out scanners, then compare Spearman correlation and Dice with U-Net.

That keeps prototype novelty scoring in place while focusing the plan on boundary uncertainty. The calibration concerns how the boundary-uncertainty signal relates to annotator disagreement on held-out scanners. The planned comparison with U-Net covers two measures: Spearman correlation and segmentation Dice. This is a plan, not a report that calibration or comparison has been completed.
What does it mean to calibrate boundary uncertainty against annotator disagreement?

The intent is for the uncertainty assigned to boundaries to reflect where annotators disagree about them. In general terms, greater disagreement should correspond to greater boundary uncertainty. The plan does not specify a calibration method or claim that the correspondence has already been achieved.
Is annotator disagreement being used to decide whether anatomy is unfamiliar?

Not in this plan. Annotator disagreement is the reference for boundary uncertainty. Prototype novelty scoring remains the separate signal concerning unfamiliar anatomy; calibrating boundary uncertainty does not make those two scores interchangeable.
Why specify held-out scanners for the boundary-uncertainty work?

The distinction between ambiguous boundaries and unfamiliar anatomy matters under acquisition-domain shift, so the plan places the boundary-uncertainty assessment in a held-out-scanner setting. It asks whether the relationship with annotator disagreement is meaningful there, rather than stating that it already generalizes across scanners.
Does the wording say which scanner or how many scanners are held out?
No. It specifies held-out scanners but gives no scanner identities, count, or rule for combining measurements across them.
Is calibration the same thing as measuring Spearman correlation?

They are related but not identical. Calibration describes the intended alignment of boundary uncertainty with annotator disagreement. Spearman correlation is a rank-based measure that can be used in the planned comparison to assess whether higher uncertainty tends to accompany higher disagreement.
